extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature, theatre historians, and actors preparing Restoration plays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative commentary embedded in an edition of Dryden's Marriage A-la-Mode, chiefly addressing how the affected character Melantha should be acted and how certain production choices (language, conclusion, publicity) affect the comedy's reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of Melantha (characterization and acting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melantha 'is as finished an impertinent as ever fluttered in a drawing-room; and seems to contain the most complete system of female foppery that could possibly be crowded into the tortured form of a fine lady.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting guidance and specifics: make language, dress, motion, manners, soul, and body in a continual hurry to be something more than necessary; show ridiculous airs on meeting a gallant (no modesty), read a letter with a 'careless dropping lip, and an erected brow,' crumble the letter in her palm, pour down 'her whole artillery of airs, eyes, and motion,' fall and rise repeatedly ('playing her chest forward in fifty falls and risings, like a swan upon waving water'), be rapidly fond of her own wit (not permitting her lover to praise it), use silent assenting bows and vain endeavours to speak; overall, render the affected, fantastical expression strongly. (This summary preserves Cibber's original descriptive examples as prescriptive acting details.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of French phrases and fashionable diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The affected lady throws French phrases into her conversation; some have been since naturalized, as 'good graces', 'minuet', 'chagrin', 'grimace', 'ridicule', and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance or text-editing, allow or render these French imports naturally as part of the character's affected speech — they mark social affectation and should be used to signal Melantha's fashionable pretensions rather than as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of abrupt/sudden turns of fortune in comic conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Little can be said of the tragic part of the drama. The sudden turn of fortune in the conclusion is ridiculed in 'The Rehearsal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative caution about plotting in comedy: avoid resolving comic plots by implausible, abrupt reversals of fortune or contrived tragic turns — such devices were subject to contemporary ridicule and may undermine comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of topical production devices to attract audiences (prologue-stage publicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: To oblige the town, the city, and the court ... We'll follow the new mode which they begin, And treat them with a room, and couch within: For that's one way, howe'er the play fall short, To oblige the town, the city, and the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical production guidance embedded in the prologue: incorporate fashionable entertainments or novelties (e.g., masking balls, special staging or reception rooms) connected to a performance to recommend the play and draw audiences — a recognized strategy to bolster a production's reception even if the play itself is imperfect.
